questions.question: The alcohol shown below is heated with acidified permanganate ($MnO_4^-/H^+$). What is the systematic name for the product of the reaction?
questions.answer: The reactant is 3-methylbutan-1-ol, a primary alcohol, which is oxidised by acidified permanganate to a carboxylic acid with the same carbon chain: 3-methylbutanoic acid (D).
options: 2-methylpentanoic acid
4-methylpentanoic acid
2-methylbutanoic acid
3-methylbutanoic acid

questions.question: Cinnamic acid is an organic substance that partly contributes to the flavour of oil of cinnamon. A structure of cinnamic acid is shown. Which of the following reagents would you expect to react with cinnamic acid under the conditions given?
questions.answer: Cinnamic acid contains a $C=C$ double bond and a carboxyl group. The $C=C$ allows addition polymerisation (copolymerisation with ethene) and addition of $Br_2$ (decolourising bromine water) at room temperature. The $-COOH$ group reacts with methanol, with sulfuric acid catalyst, in esterification to form methyl cinnamate. All three reactions occur (A).
options: $CH_2CH_2$ and catalyst: Yes; $Br_2(aq)$ at room temperature: Yes; $CH_3OH$ and $H_2SO_4$ catalyst: Yes
$CH_2CH_2$ and catalyst: Yes; $Br_2(aq)$ at room temperature: No; $CH_3OH$ and $H_2SO_4$ catalyst: Yes
$CH_2CH_2$ and catalyst: No; $Br_2(aq)$ at room temperature: Yes; $CH_3OH$ and $H_2SO_4$ catalyst: Yes
$CH_2CH_2$ and catalyst: No; $Br_2(aq)$ at room temperature: Yes; $CH_3OH$ and $H_2SO_4$ catalyst: No

questions.question: The general formula of a triglyceride is shown. Which one of the following equations represents the hydrolysis of a triglyceride?
questions.answer: Hydrolysis of a triglyceride is the reaction with three molecules of water: water adds across each ester linkage to form glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol, with three $-OH$ groups) and three carboxylic acid ($RCOOH$) molecules (A).
options: ![A](assets/img/chem-2022-baulkham-hills/q3a.png)
![B](assets/img/chem-2022-baulkham-hills/q3b.png)
![C](assets/img/chem-2022-baulkham-hills/q3c.png)
![D](assets/img/chem-2022-baulkham-hills/q3d.png)

questions.question: A liquid mixture of 50% ethanol and 50% water was distilled in the apparatus shown. The boiling point of ethanol is $78^\circ$C and that of water is $100^\circ$C. As the mixture was heated, the temperature shown by the thermometer initially rose but then remained constant at $78^\circ$C for some time. Which one of the following statements about the percentage of ethanol in the vapours at points $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ (up the fractionating column), when the temperature is at a constant $78^\circ$C, is true?
questions.answer: The column is cooler higher up. As the vapour rises, the less volatile component (water) condenses and runs back down, while the more volatile ethanol continues up. The proportion of ethanol in the vapour therefore increases from $X$ to $Y$ to $Z$ (B).
options: The percentage of ethanol in the vapours at $X$ is equal to 50%.
The percentages of ethanol in the vapours increase in order at positions $X$, $Y$ and $Z$.
The percentages of ethanol in the vapours at $Y$ and $Z$ are equal but greater than at $X$.
The percentages of ethanol in the vapours at $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are equal but greater than 50%.

questions.question: The diagram shows the structural formula of prop-1-ene. How many signals would it show in $^{13}$C NMR and proton ($^1$H) NMR?
questions.answer: There are three carbon environments ($CH_3$, $=CH-$ and $=CH_2$), so three $^{13}C$ signals. In the proton spectrum the $CH_3$ hydrogens give one signal and the $=CH-$ hydrogen gives another. The two hydrogens on the $=CH_2$ carbon are not equivalent (one is cis and one trans to the methyl group, because rotation about the double bond is restricted), so they give two separate signals. Total: 4 proton signals and 3 carbon signals (D).
options: Proton NMR: 3; C-13 NMR: 3
Proton NMR: 4; C-13 NMR: 4
Proton NMR: 3; C-13 NMR: 4
Proton NMR: 4; C-13 NMR: 3

questions.question: Nitrogen dioxide (a brown gas) and dinitrogen tetroxide (a colourless gas) are both oxides of nitrogen. They are in equilibrium according to the equation $2NO_2(g)\rightleftharpoons N_2O_4(g)$. An equilibrium mixture of the two gases at room temperature is light brown but at higher temperatures the colour becomes a much deeper brown. What conclusion can be drawn from this observation?
questions.answer: Raising the temperature produces more brown $NO_2$, so the equilibrium shifts to the left. By Le Chatelier's principle, the system opposes the temperature rise by absorbing heat, so the reverse reaction is endothermic (and the forward reaction is exothermic) (A).
options: The reverse reaction in the equation is endothermic.
The forward reaction in the equation is endothermic.
The brown colour is due to the strong nitrogen–oxygen bonds in $NO_2$.
The equilibrium concentration of $N_2O_4$ is not dependent on temperature.

questions.question: Hydrogen gas reacts with iodine gas to form hydrogen iodide according to the equation $H_2(g)+I_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2HI(g)$ at 700 K. At equilibrium, the concentrations of $H_2$, $I_2$ and $HI$ are $0.214$, $0.214$ and $1.57$ mol L$^{-1}$ respectively. What is the value of the equilibrium constant for this reaction?
What will happen when sulfuric acid is added to a saturated solution of the sparingly soluble calcium sulfate? ($K_{sp}(CaSO_4)=2.4\times10^{-5}$)
questions.answer: In the saturated solution $CaSO_4(s)\rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)$ and $K_{sp}=[Ca^{2+}][SO_4^{2-}]$. Sulfuric acid adds $SO_4^{2-}$ (common ion), so the ionic product exceeds $K_{sp}$ and the equilibrium shifts to the left (Le Chatelier), precipitating $CaSO_4$. The ion concentrations then decrease over time until $[Ca^{2+}][SO_4^{2-}]=K_{sp}$ again. The $H^+$ ions have no effect (D).
options: The concentration of calcium and sulfate ions will increase over time due to the presence of $H^+$ ions.
The concentration of calcium and sulfate ions will decrease over time due to the presence of $H^+$ ions.
The concentration of calcium and sulfate ions will increase over time due to the presence of $SO_4^{2-}$ ions.
The concentration of calcium and sulfate ions will decrease over time due to the presence of $SO_4^{2-}$ ions.

questions.question: At a certain temperature, $K_{eq}$ for the reaction $2O_3(g)\rightleftharpoons3O_2(g)$ is 75. $0.3$ mol of $O_3$ and $1.5$ mol of $O_2$ were introduced into a 5 L reaction vessel. Which row correctly identifies the direction of the equilibrium shift and the reason for the shift?
questions.answer: $[O_3]=\frac{0.3}{5}=0.06$ M and $[O_2]=\frac{1.5}{5}=0.30$ M. $Q=\dfrac{[O_2]^3}{[O_3]^2}=\dfrac{(0.30)^3}{(0.06)^2}=7.5$. Since $Q<K_{eq}=75$, the system must shift to the right (towards products) to reach equilibrium (D).
options: Left; $Q>K_{eq}$
Left; $Q<K_{eq}$
Right; $Q>K_{eq}$
Right; $Q<K_{eq}$

questions.question: Hydrogen is produced on an industrial scale from methane by the reaction $2H_2O(g)+CH_4(g)\rightleftharpoons CO_2(g)+4H_2(g)$. If an inert gas is added to the equilibrium system at constant temperature and constant volume, the concentration of $H_2$ will
questions.answer: Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not change the concentration (or partial pressure) of any reacting species, so $Q$ is unchanged and still equals $K$. The equilibrium is not disturbed and $[H_2]$ does not change (C).
options: increase.
decrease.
not change.
decrease then increase.

questions.question: The sulfate ($SO_4^{2-}$) content of a plant fertiliser is to be determined by gravimetric analysis of a 2.5 g sample of fertiliser. The first part of this analysis would involve
questions.answer: The sulfate in the solid fertiliser must first be brought into solution (dissolved in water, with any insoluble material then filtered off) so that all the $SO_4^{2-}$ is available to react with the precipitating reagent (C).
options: producing a precipitate
filtering the sulfate ions from the insoluble material in the fertiliser
dissolving the sulfate from the fertiliser into water
adding an indicator to an aliquot of the sulfate solution

questions.question: In the gravimetric analysis of the sulfate in a fertiliser, an excess solution is added to produce a precipitate. This solution is known as the precipitating reagent. Which precipitating reagent would be the most suitable for this analysis?
questions.answer: Barium ions form the insoluble precipitate $BaSO_4$ with sulfate: $Ba^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)\to BaSO_4(s)$. $Na^+$, $K^+$ and $Cu^{2+}$ sulfates are all soluble, and $CuSO_4$ would add sulfate rather than precipitate it (B).
options: $NaCl(aq)$
$KCl(aq)$
$CuSO_4(aq)$

questions.question: In the gravimetric analysis of the sulfate in a fertiliser, which of the following errors in experimental procedure would produce a percentage of sulfate in the fertiliser that is LESS than the true value?
questions.answer: If excess precipitating reagent is not added, not all of the sulfate precipitates, so the mass of precipitate is too low and the calculated percentage of sulfate is too low (C). Not washing the precipitate leaves soluble impurities, and not drying it fully leaves water, so in both cases the measured mass is too high.
options: Failure to wash the precipitate with distilled water.
Failure to dry the precipitate to a constant mass.
Failure to add an excess amount of precipitating reagent.
Failure to let the precipitate dry in an oven.

questions.question: A 20 mL aliquot of vinegar is titrated with $15$ mL of $0.10$ M NaOH. The vinegar is in the conical flask ($B$) and the NaOH is in the burette ($A$). The piece of equipment labelled $A$ should be
questions.answer: $A$ is the burette, which contains the titrant. It should be rinsed with the solution it is to deliver ($0.10$ M NaOH) so that residual water does not dilute the titrant, and then filled with that solution (C).
options: rinsed with distilled water and filled with 20 mL of vinegar
rinsed with distilled water and filled with 0.10 M NaOH.
rinsed with 0.10 M NaOH and filled with 0.10 M NaOH
rinsed with vinegar and filled with 20 mL of vinegar

questions.question: A 20 mL aliquot of vinegar (in the conical flask, $B$) is titrated with $0.10$ M NaOH from the burette ($A$); the titre is $15$ mL when the equipment is prepared correctly. If the equipment labelled $A$ (the burette) is rinsed with distilled water only before the titration,
questions.answer: The water left in the burette dilutes the NaOH, so the concentration of the titrant is lower than $0.10$ M. A larger volume of the diluted NaOH is therefore needed to neutralise the same amount of acetic acid, so the titre is greater than 15 mL (C).
options: the volume of NaOH used will be 15 mL
the volume of vinegar used will be less than 15 mL
the volume of NaOH used will be greater than 15 mL
the volume of NaOH used will be exactly 20 mL

questions.question: A 20 mL aliquot of vinegar is pipetted into a conical flask ($B$) and titrated with $0.10$ M NaOH from the burette; the titre is $15$ mL when the equipment is prepared correctly. If the equipment labelled $B$ (the conical flask) is rinsed with distilled water before the titration,
questions.answer: Water in the conical flask does not change the number of moles of acid that were pipetted into it, so the volume of NaOH needed to neutralise it is unchanged (A).
options: the volume of NaOH used will be 15 mL
the volume of vinegar used will be less than 15 mL
the volume of NaOH used will be greater than 15 mL
the volume of NaOH used will be exactly 20 mL

questions.question: Which of the following rows correctly corresponds with the symbols that describe the thermodynamic properties of a system?
questions.answer: $\Delta G$ is the change in Gibbs free energy, $\Delta H$ is the change in heat content (enthalpy) and $\Delta S$ is the change in randomness (entropy) (A).
options: $\Delta G$: change in Gibbs free energy; $\Delta H$: change in heat content; $\Delta S$: change in randomness
$\Delta G$: total Gibbs free energy; $\Delta H$: total heat content; $\Delta S$: total randomness
$\Delta G$: initial Gibbs free energy; $\Delta H$: initial heat content; $\Delta S$: initial randomness
$\Delta G$: change in randomness; $\Delta H$: change in Gibbs free energy; $\Delta S$: change in heat content

questions.question: For a chemical equilibrium $A+B\rightleftharpoons2C$, the value of the equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$) is $4.2\times10^{-5}$. What is the value of the equilibrium constant for the reverse reaction?
questions.answer: The equilibrium constant for the reverse reaction is the reciprocal: $K_{rev}=\dfrac{1}{4.2\times10^{-5}}=2.38\times10^{4}$ (C).

questions.question: When an ionic solid dissolves in water and forms a saturated solution, the process can be described in stages. These stages include: I. When two opposing rates are equal, the system reaches equilibrium. II. Aqueous ions arrive at the solid lattice and become part of it. III. The ionic lattice dissociates into individual ions. IV. The ionic lattice is surrounded by water molecules. Which of the following gives the correct order of stages?
questions.answer:
Dissolving begins when the lattice is surrounded by water molecules (IV), and the system ends when the opposing rates of dissolving and re-crystallising are equal and equilibrium is reached (I). Dissociation of the lattice (III) and ions returning to the lattice (II) occur in between, once dissolving has begun and as equilibrium is approached. Only C begins with IV and ends with I (C).

Note: strictly, the chemical order is IV, III, II, I; none of the options gives that order, but C is the only one starting with IV and ending with I.
options: I, II, III, IV
III, I, IV, II
IV, II, III, I
II, IV, I, III

questions.question: The diagram shows a portion of a polymer. Which of the structures represents the monomer?
questions.answer: The polymer is an addition polymer with a $-CH_2-CH(COOH)-$ repeating unit. Its monomer is an alkene with a carboxylic acid group, $CH_2=CH-COOH$ (propenoic/acrylic acid), which is structure D. The other structures have the wrong number of bonds on one or more atoms or the wrong connectivity.
options: ![A](assets/img/chem-2022-baulkham-hills/q20a.png)
![B](assets/img/chem-2022-baulkham-hills/q20b.png)
![C](assets/img/chem-2022-baulkham-hills/q20c.png)
![D](assets/img/chem-2022-baulkham-hills/q20d.png)

questions.question: Carbon monoxide, $CO$, reacts with ammonia, $NH_3$, to produce highly toxic hydrogen cyanide, $HCN$, as well as carbon dioxide and hydrogen. The reaction is endothermic: $2CO(g)+NH_3(g)\rightleftharpoons HCN(g)+CO_2(g)+H_2(g)$. Write the expression for the equilibrium constant for this reaction.

Carbon monoxide reacts with ammonia: $2CO(g)+NH_3(g)\rightleftharpoons HCN(g)+CO_2(g)+H_2(g)$. In one experiment, a mixture of $CO$ and $NH_3$, together with a suitable catalyst, was injected into a sealed 100 mL gas syringe and allowed to come to equilibrium. The equilibrium mixture contained $[CO]=0.0025$ M, $[NH_3]=0.00125$ M and $[HCN]=0.0042$ M. (The $HCN$, $CO_2$ and $H_2$ were formed only from this reaction, in a 1:1:1 ratio.) Calculate the equilibrium constant for the reaction at this temperature.

Analysts investigated the effect of two different changes on the equilibrium system $2CO(g)+NH_3(g)\rightleftharpoons HCN(g)+CO_2(g)+H_2(g)$ (endothermic) by monitoring the amount of $HCN$ (in moles) present in the gas mixture. State whether the amount of $HCN$ will increase, decrease or have no effect for each change: (1) halving the volume of the gas mixture, keeping the temperature constant; (2) returning the volume of the gas mixture to 100 mL and then injecting some powdered palladium into the gas syringe (palladium absorbs $H_2$ gas onto its surface).
questions.answer: (1) No effect. There are 3 mol of gas on each side of the equation, so changing the volume (pressure) does not favour either direction. (2) Increase. Palladium removes $H_2$, a product, so the equilibrium shifts to the right to replace it, producing more $HCN$.

questions.question: At equilibrium in a 100 mL gas syringe the concentrations are $[HCN]=0.0042$ M and $[NH_3]=0.00125$ M for the system $2CO(g)+NH_3(g)\rightleftharpoons HCN(g)+CO_2(g)+H_2(g)$. Complete the concentration–time graph on the axes provided to show what will happen to the concentrations of $HCN$ and $NH_3$ in the equilibrium mixture when the volume of the gas mixture is suddenly halved at constant temperature.
questions.answer:
Halving the volume instantly doubles every concentration: $[HCN]$ rises from $0.0042$ M to $0.0084$ M and $[NH_3]$ from $0.00125$ M to $0.0025$ M. There are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side, so there is no shift in equilibrium afterwards and both concentrations stay constant at these new values.

Note: the marking guide gives the final $[NH_3]$ as 0.0026 M; doubling 0.00125 M gives 0.0025 M.

questions.question: $CO$ gas is produced when a hydrocarbon fuel, such as butane, $C_4H_{10}$, is burnt in a limited air supply. Write the balanced equation for the combustion of $C_4H_{10}$ in a limited air supply, assuming that $CO$ is the only carbon-based oxidation product.

Haemoglobin in red blood cells takes up $O_2$ from the air in an equilibrium reaction (Equation 1): $Hb_4(aq)+4O_2(aq)\rightleftharpoons Hb_4O_8(aq)$, with equilibrium constant $K_1$. $CO$ molecules can also attach to haemoglobin (Equation 2): $Hb_4(aq)+4CO(aq)\rightleftharpoons Hb_4(CO)_4(aq)$, with equilibrium constant $K_2$. If the concentration of $CO$ in the air inside a burning building increases to 800 ppm, anyone exposed to it will quickly lose consciousness, even if oxygen is present. To revive them, they must be given pure oxygen. What conclusions can be made about the relative values of the equilibrium constants $K_1$ and $K_2$?
questions.answer: $K_2$ is much larger than $K_1$ ($K_2\gg K_1$). $CO$ and $O_2$ compete for the haemoglobin, and even at a very low concentration of $CO$ (800 ppm, compared with about 21% $O_2$ in air) the $CO$ binds in preference to $O_2$ and the haemoglobin–$CO$ complex dominates. For this to happen, the position of equilibrium of Equation 2 must lie much further to the right than that of Equation 1, which means a much greater equilibrium constant. (Giving pure $O_2$ raises $[O_2]$ enough to shift Equation 1 to the right and displace the $CO$.)

questions.question: Claire is analysing a sample of paint to determine the organic solvents that are present. She separates the compounds and analyses each using infra-red (IR) spectroscopy and $^{13}$C and $^1$H NMR spectroscopy. One compound has the molecular formula $C_5H_{10}O$. The IR spectrum of this compound is shown. From the IR spectrum, identify the organic family to which this compound belongs. Justify your answer by referring to the relevant wave number.
questions.answer: The compound is a ketone or an aldehyde. The strong, sharp absorption at about $1700$ cm$^{-1}$ corresponds to a $C=O$ (carbonyl) group (aldehydes $1660$–$1745$ cm$^{-1}$, ketones $1680$–$1850$ cm$^{-1}$). There is no broad $O-H$ absorption at $3230$–$3550$ cm$^{-1}$ (or $2500$–$3000$ cm$^{-1}$), so it is not an alcohol or a carboxylic acid. With only one oxygen atom in $C_5H_{10}O$ it cannot be an ester or carboxylic acid. The peak near $3000$ cm$^{-1}$ is the $C-H$ stretch, present in all organic families.

questions.question: Claire isolates a compound with the molecular formula $C_5H_{10}O$ from a sample of paint. Its IR spectrum shows a strong absorption at about $1700$ cm$^{-1}$ (a carbonyl group) and no $O-H$ absorption. Its $^{13}$C NMR spectrum has peaks at about $215$, $35$ and $9$ ppm. Its $^1$H NMR spectrum has two peaks: at $1.0$ ppm (splitting pattern: 3, i.e. a triplet) and $2.4$ ppm (splitting pattern: 4, i.e. a quartet). The spectra are shown. Draw a structural formula for this compound that is consistent with the data provided, and explain your reasoning by referring to the data.
questions.answer: The compound is pentan-3-one, $CH_3CH_2COCH_2CH_3$. **Symmetry:** $C_5H_{10}O$ has five carbons but the $^{13}C$ spectrum shows only three peaks, so some carbons are in the same environment, and the $^1H$ spectrum has only two peaks, so there are only two hydrogen environments. This indicates a symmetrical molecule. **$^{13}C$ NMR:** the peak at $215$ ppm is a carbonyl carbon in a ketone ($R_2C=O$, $205$–$220$ ppm); $35$ ppm is a $R-CH_2-R$ carbon ($20$–$45$ ppm); $9$ ppm is a $R-CH_3$ carbon ($8$–$25$ ppm). **$^1H$ NMR:** the $1.0$ ppm peak is a $R-CH_3$ ($0.9$–$1.0$ ppm), split into a triplet by the two hydrogens on the adjacent $CH_2$; the $2.4$ ppm peak is $-CH_2-$ next to the carbonyl ($R-CO-CH_2-$, $2.1$–$2.7$ ppm), split into a quartet by the three hydrogens of the adjacent $CH_3$. This fits $CH_3CH_2-CO-CH_2CH_3$ only; an aldehyde would give more than three carbon environments.

questions.question: Using IUPAC nomenclature, name the three compounds shown (Compound 1, Compound 2 and Compound 3).
questions.answer: Compound 1: propan-1-amine ($CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2$). Compound 2: 2,2-dimethylpropane ($C(CH_3)_4$). Compound 3: propanamide ($CH_3CH_2CONH_2$).

questions.question: Compound 1 is propan-1-amine ($CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2$), Compound 2 is 2,2-dimethylpropane ($C(CH_3)_4$) and Compound 3 is propanamide ($CH_3CH_2CONH_2$). Compare the intermolecular forces in these three molecules and predict the order of boiling points (lowest to highest) of these molecules. Explain your predictions.
questions.answer: Order of increasing boiling point: Compound 2 < Compound 1 < Compound 3. The stronger the intermolecular forces, the more energy needed to separate the molecules, so the higher the boiling point. Compound 2 is a non-polar alkane with only weak dispersion forces. Compound 1 is a primary amine: the polar $N-H$ bonds allow hydrogen bonding between molecules (stronger than dispersion forces) as well as dispersion forces. Compound 3 is an amide with a very polar $-CONH_2$ group: the $N-H$ hydrogens bond to the $C=O$ oxygen of neighbouring molecules, and the planar group allows two hydrogen bonds between a pair of molecules (forming dimers or a network), so it has the strongest intermolecular forces and the highest boiling point.

questions.question: Compound 3 is propanamide, $CH_3CH_2CONH_2$. Identify how compound 3 could be produced by a chemical reaction. Include an equation in your response.
questions.answer: React propanoic acid with ammonia and heat the mixture (the ammonium propanoate salt formed dehydrates): $CH_3CH_2COOH+NH_3\to CH_3CH_2CONH_2+H_2O$.

questions.question: The table shows acid dissociation constants at $25^\circ$C. Identify the weakest acid in the table and determine the $pK_a$ value for this acid.
questions.answer:
The weakest acid has the smallest $K_a$: water, $H_2O$ ($K_a=1.0\times10^{-14}$). $pK_a=-\log_{10}(1.0\times10^{-14})=14.00$.

Note: the table's value for water is used; the data-sheet value of $K_a$ for water is $K_w$.

questions.question: Hydrocyanic acid ($HCN$) has $K_a=6.2\times10^{-10}$ at $25^\circ$C. Calculate the pH of a $0.10$ M solution of hydrocyanic acid.
questions.answer: $HCN(aq)+H_2O(l)\rightleftharpoons CN^-(aq)+H_3O^+(aq)$, $K_a=\dfrac{[CN^-][H_3O^+]}{[HCN]}=6.2\times10^{-10}$. Let $[H_3O^+]=x$, then $[CN^-]=x$ and $[HCN]=0.10-x\approx0.10$ (since $x$ is very small). $x^2=(6.2\times10^{-10})(0.10)=6.2\times10^{-11}$, so $[H_3O^+]=7.87\times10^{-6}$ M and $pH=-\log_{10}(7.87\times10^{-6})=5.10$.

questions.question: A buffer solution is prepared by combining $100$ mL of $0.10$ M $HCN$ and $100$ mL of $0.10$ M $NaCN$. Given $K_a(HCN)=6.2\times10^{-10}$, calculate the pH of this buffer solution and explain the classification of the solution as a buffer.
questions.answer: On mixing, the volume doubles, so $[HCN]=[CN^-]=0.050$ M. $K_a=\dfrac{[CN^-][H_3O^+]}{[HCN]}$ gives $[H_3O^+]=K_a\dfrac{[HCN]}{[CN^-]}=6.2\times10^{-10}\times\dfrac{0.050}{0.050}=6.2\times10^{-10}$ M, so $pH=9.21$. The solution is a buffer because it contains a weak acid ($HCN$) and its conjugate base ($CN^-$) in comparable concentrations, so it resists changes in pH when small amounts of strong acid or base are added. Added $H^+$ is consumed by $CN^-$ ($CN^-+H^+\to HCN$) and added $OH^-$ is consumed by $HCN$ ($HCN+OH^-\to CN^-+H_2O$). The ratio $[HCN]/[CN^-]$ changes only slightly, so the pH stays close to $9.21$.

questions.question: A solution contains four cations: $Ag^+$, $Ba^{2+}$, $Ca^{2+}$ and $Fe^{2+}$. The flow chart represents the steps taken to identify each cation: the mixture is treated with excess $HCl$ and filtered (precipitate 1, filtrate 1); filtrate 1 is treated with excess $NH_3$ and filtered (precipitate 2, filtrate 2); filtrate 2 is treated with $H_2SO_4$ and filtered (precipitate 3, filtrate 3). Name precipitates 1, 2 and 3 and write the ionic equation for the formation of each precipitate. Suggest a test to confirm the identity of the remaining cation in filtrate 3.
questions.answer:
Precipitate 1 is silver chloride, $AgCl$: $Ag^+(aq)+Cl^-(aq)\to AgCl(s)$. Precipitate 2 is iron(II) hydroxide, $Fe(OH)_2$: $Fe^{2+}(aq)+2OH^-(aq)\to Fe(OH)_2(s)$ (the $OH^-$ comes from the ammonia solution). Precipitate 3 is barium sulfate, $BaSO_4$: $Ba^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)\to BaSO_4(s)$. The remaining cation in filtrate 3 is $Ca^{2+}$. Test: a flame test, giving an orange-red flame (or add $NaOH$ solution, which gives a white precipitate of $Ca(OH)_2$ that does not dissolve in excess).

Note: the marking guide's equations for precipitates 2 and 3 were unbalanced or had the wrong charge ($Fe^{2+}+OH^-$ and $SO_4^{2+}$); the balanced equations are given above.

questions.question: Different tests are used to distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols. Describe ONE test for each type of alcohol and include the chemical reaction.
questions.answer:
Heat the alcohol with an oxidising agent such as acidified potassium permanganate ($KMnO_4/H^+$, purple to colourless) or acidified potassium dichromate (orange to green). **Primary alcohol** (e.g. ethanol): the oxidant is decolourised as the alcohol is oxidised, via the aldehyde, to a carboxylic acid: $CH_3CH_2OH+2[O]\to CH_3COOH+H_2O$. The acid can be confirmed by adding a carbonate: effervescence of $CO_2$ gas, $2CH_3COOH+Na_2CO_3\to2CH_3COONa+CO_2+H_2O$. **Secondary alcohol** (e.g. propan-2-ol): the oxidant is also decolourised, forming a ketone: $CH_3CH(OH)CH_3+[O]\to CH_3COCH_3+H_2O$. No gas is produced when a carbonate is added (no acid). **Tertiary alcohol**: no reaction with the oxidising agent, so the solution remains purple (or orange).

Note: the marking guide's carbonate equation was not balanced; the balanced equation is shown.

questions.question: The $K_{sp}$ value for magnesium hydroxide is $5.61\times10^{-12}$. Write the equation for the solubility equilibrium for magnesium hydroxide.
questions.answer: $Mg(OH)_2(s)\rightleftharpoons Mg^{2+}(aq)+2OH^-(aq)$

questions.question: Write the $K_{sp}$ expression for magnesium hydroxide, $Mg(OH)_2$.
The $K_{sp}$ value for magnesium hydroxide is $5.61\times10^{-12}$ at $25^\circ$C. Calculate the solubility of magnesium hydroxide at $25^\circ$C.
questions.answer: Let the solubility be $x$ mol L$^{-1}$. $Mg(OH)_2(s)\rightleftharpoons Mg^{2+}(aq)+2OH^-(aq)$ gives $[Mg^{2+}]=x$ and $[OH^-]=2x$. $K_{sp}=x(2x)^2=4x^3=5.61\times10^{-12}$, so $x^3=1.4025\times10^{-12}$ and $x=1.12\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$. (So $[OH^-]=2.24\times10^{-4}$ M.)

questions.question:
A green leaf with a mass of $0.320$ g is analysed for its chlorophyll content by UV–visible spectroscopy. The chlorophyll is extracted and dissolved in $250$ mL of solvent. A sample of the solution is placed in a UV–visible spectrometer with the wavelength set at $410$ nm. The absorbance of the chlorophyll solution at this wavelength is $0.21$. The absorbance values of four standard chlorophyll solutions are:

| Concentration (M) | Absorbance |
|---|---|
| $2.5\\times10^{-4}$ | $0.120$ |
| $5.0\\times10^{-4}$ | $0.239$ |
| $7.5\\times10^{-4}$ | $0.351$ |
| $1.0\\times10^{-3}$ | $0.483$ |

Using the grid provided, construct a calibration graph showing the absorbance of the chlorophyll standards.
questions.answer: Plot absorbance (vertical axis, 0 to 0.60) against concentration in M (horizontal axis, 0 to 0.0012) with a suitable scale, mark the four points accurately and draw a straight line of best fit through them (it passes very close to the origin). The graph shows a linear relationship, as expected from the Beer–Lambert law.

questions.question: A calibration line for chlorophyll at $410$ nm is a straight line through the points ($2.5\times10^{-4}$ M, $0.120$), ($5.0\times10^{-4}$ M, $0.239$), ($7.5\times10^{-4}$ M, $0.351$) and ($1.0\times10^{-3}$ M, $0.483$). The chlorophyll solution extracted from a leaf (250 mL) has an absorbance of $0.21$ at this wavelength. What is the concentration of chlorophyll in g L$^{-1}$ in the 250 mL solution? $M_r$(chlorophyll) $=893.5$ g mol$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
From the line of best fit (gradient about $480$ M$^{-1}$), an absorbance of $0.21$ corresponds to $c\approx4.4\times10^{-4}$ M. Concentration in g L$^{-1}$ $=4.4\times10^{-4}\times893.5=0.39$ g L$^{-1}$.

Note: readings from the graph of $4.2$–$4.4\times10^{-4}$ M are acceptable; the marking guide read $4.2\times10^{-4}$ M, giving $0.375$ g L$^{-1}$ (its working line also printed $0.384$ g L$^{-1}$, an arithmetic slip).

questions.question: The chlorophyll from a $0.320$ g green leaf was dissolved in $250$ mL of solvent, giving a concentration of $0.39$ g L$^{-1}$ (determined by UV–visible spectroscopy). What is the percentage by mass of chlorophyll in the leaf?
questions.answer:
Mass of chlorophyll $=0.39\ \text{g L}^{-1}\times0.250\ \text{L}=0.0985$ g (about $0.098$ g). Percentage by mass $=\dfrac{0.0985}{0.320}\times100=31\%$ (about 30.8%).

Note: using the marking guide's $0.375$ g L$^{-1}$ gives $0.0938$ g and $29.3\%$, which is also acceptable.

questions.question: Why was light with a wavelength of $410$ nm chosen for the UV–visible analysis of chlorophyll?
questions.answer: Chlorophyll absorbs strongly at about $410$ nm (violet/blue light), so this wavelength gives the highest absorbance (greatest sensitivity) for a measurable change with concentration.

questions.question: A solution of hydrochloric acid was standardised by titration against sodium carbonate solution. All glassware was rinsed correctly to remove possible contamination; hydrochloric acid was placed in the burette and $25.0$ mL of sodium carbonate solution was pipetted into the conical flask. Identify the chemical used to rinse the pipette and justify your answer.
questions.answer: The pipette should be rinsed with the sodium carbonate solution. Rinsing with water would dilute the solution that is drawn into the pipette, changing the number of moles of sodium carbonate delivered and making the standardisation inaccurate. Rinsing with the sodium carbonate solution ensures that any residue in the pipette has the same concentration.

questions.question: A solution of hydrochloric acid was standardised by titration against sodium carbonate solution. Explain why sodium carbonate solution, rather than sodium hydroxide solution, is used to standardise the hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer: Standardisation requires a primary standard: a substance that can be obtained pure, is stable, does not absorb water or react with $CO_2$ in the air, can be weighed accurately and has a relatively high molar mass (to minimise weighing error). Sodium carbonate meets these requirements ($M=106$ g mol$^{-1}$). Sodium hydroxide absorbs water and reacts with atmospheric $CO_2$, is not available as a pure stable solid, and has a lower molar mass ($40$ g mol$^{-1}$), so a solution of exactly known concentration cannot be made by weighing it.

questions.question: Seashells contain a mixture of carbonate compounds. Standard hydrochloric acid ($0.200$ mol L$^{-1}$) was used to determine the percentage by mass of carbonate ions in a seashell. A $0.154$ g sample of the seashell was placed in a conical flask and $50.0$ mL of the standardised hydrochloric acid was added. At the completion of the reaction, the mixture in the flask was titrated with $0.250$ mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide, and $29.5$ mL of sodium hydroxide was used. Calculate the percentage by mass of carbonate ions in the sample of the seashell.
questions.answer:
$CO_3^{2-}+2HCl\to2Cl^-+CO_2+H_2O$. $n(HCl)_{added}=0.200\times0.0500=0.0100$ mol. $n(NaOH)=0.250\times0.0295=0.007375$ mol $=n(HCl)_{excess}$. $n(HCl)_{reacted}=0.0100-0.007375=0.002625$ mol. $n(CO_3^{2-})=\frac12\times0.002625=0.0013125$ mol. $m(CO_3^{2-})=0.0013125\times60.01=0.0788$ g. Percentage $=\dfrac{0.0788}{0.154}\times100=51.1\%$.

Note: the marking guide gives 51.2% (rounding the mass first); answers of 51.1–51.2% were accepted.

questions.question: A student was researching calcium sulfate ($CaSO_4$) and calcium carbonate ($CaCO_3$). Their first step was to look at the solubility constants ($K_{sp}$) for the two compounds: $K_{sp}(CaSO_4)=4.93\times10^{-5}$ and $K_{sp}(CaCO_3)\approx3.4\times10^{-9}$ at $25^\circ$C. Discuss the solubilities of these two compounds at $25^\circ$C.
questions.answer: Both compounds are sparingly soluble (small $K_{sp}$ values). For each, $K_{sp}=[Ca^{2+}][anion]$, and because they have the same 1:1 stoichiometry, the $K_{sp}$ values can be compared directly. $CaSO_4$ has the much larger $K_{sp}$ ($4.93\times10^{-5}$ compared with $\sim3.4\times10^{-9}$), so it is considerably more soluble than $CaCO_3$.

questions.question: Derive the equilibrium expression for calcium sulfate and use this to calculate the solubility (in mol L$^{-1}$) of calcium sulfate. $K_{sp}(CaSO_4)=4.93\times10^{-5}$. Show your working.
questions.answer: $CaSO_4(s)\rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)$, so $K_{sp}=[Ca^{2+}][SO_4^{2-}]$. If the solubility is $s$ then $[Ca^{2+}]=[SO_4^{2-}]=s$, so $s^2=4.93\times10^{-5}$ and $s=\sqrt{4.93\times10^{-5}}=7.02\times10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Outline ONE practice of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples that uses solubility equilibria.
questions.answer: Some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander groups in northern Australia use cycad seeds as a food source. The seeds contain toxins that make them poisonous if eaten untreated. The toxins are much more soluble in water than the nutrients in the seeds, so prolonged soaking or leaching of the seeds in (running) water removes the toxins by dissolving them, leaving the less soluble nutrients behind.

questions.question: $20$ mL of $0.010$ mol L$^{-1}$ calcium nitrate is added to $20$ mL of $0.010$ mol L$^{-1}$ sodium sulfate. Determine whether precipitation of calcium sulfate will occur. ($K_{sp}(CaSO_4)=4.93\times10^{-5}$)
questions.answer: $n(Ca^{2+})=0.010\times0.020=2.0\times10^{-4}$ mol and $n(SO_4^{2-})=0.010\times0.020=2.0\times10^{-4}$ mol. The total volume is $40$ mL $=0.040$ L, so $[Ca^{2+}]=[SO_4^{2-}]=\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-4}}{0.040}=5.0\times10^{-3}$ M. Ionic product $=[Ca^{2+}][SO_4^{2-}]=(5.0\times10^{-3})^2=2.5\times10^{-5}$. Since $2.5\times10^{-5}<K_{sp}=4.93\times10^{-5}$, the solution is unsaturated and no precipitate will form.

questions.question: Label each of the detergents shown as anionic, cationic or non-ionic: (i) cetyltrimethylammonium bromide, (ii) the sodium salt of a steroid-based carboxylic acid (a bile salt), (iii) sodium alkylbenzenesulfonate.
questions.answer:
(i) Cationic: the hydrophilic head is a positively charged quaternary ammonium ion. (ii) Anionic: the hydrophilic head is a negatively charged carboxylate group ($-COO^-Na^+$). (iii) Anionic: the head is a negatively charged sulfonate group ($-SO_3^-Na^+$).

Note: the marking guide labelled (ii) non-ionic, but the structure is a sodium carboxylate, so it is anionic.

questions.question: Soaps can remove fats and oils from the skin because of their structure. Discuss this statement.
questions.answer: Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid. It has a non-polar, hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail, which is attracted to fats and oils (dispersion forces), and a negatively charged, hydrophilic carboxylate head, which is attracted to water (ion–dipole forces). When soap is rubbed on the skin with water, the tails dissolve into the oil or grease and the heads stay in the water, so the oil is surrounded by soap molecules, forming spherical micelles with the heads on the outside. The micelles are dispersed in the water and rinsed away. Soap is also a surfactant that reduces the surface tension of water, helping the water wet the skin. This dual structure is what allows soap to remove fats and oils.
